comments.body: @skipperdogman  Any animal that is a subspecies (Sus scrofa domesticus) has to also be the species (Sus scrofa). Tagging to either species or subspecies is considered acceptable on iNaturalist.

@skipperdogman to piggyback off of @maxallen , even when only discussing the admixture between purely feralized domestics in NZ, we are still dealing with a genetic history made up of domestic breeds from Europe and from Asia, which do not share a common 'domestic' ancestor. I realize after a point it might seem like stupid, but the fact that even at a domestic level they do not come from the same common 'stock', yet all have a feralized morphology, it seems best (in my opinion, which I realize a lot of you don't hold in high regard lol) to keep it at the species level

Thanks @elliotgreiner 
@tony_wills Do you know why wild pigs in NZ are identified to ssp.?
I used to do that, adamant that no one introduced anything other than domestic pig stock into NZ (why would they??!!) ... but read comments on /observations/1194105

Razor backs can make amazing pets if raised with people and some wild ones can be 'tamed' easily enough. 
Some wild pigs out there are rather colourful which would suggest domestic breeds have been 'hybridizing' with them.
Thanks All for the comments and link to interesting comments info. Will stick to Sus Scrofa from now on since I'm not qualified to determine ssp.
After a lot of reading, I think Domestic Pig is fine after all.
@jacqui-nz it doesn't look like you need to know particular details of the pig's ancestry as all the various subspecies mixed together are covered by Sus scrofa ssp. domesticus.
Only domestic stock were brought to NZ, so these pigs can not be ID'd as anything other than Sus scrofa ssp. domesticus

No pure "wild boar" in nz. That is a distinct European species found in the wild in forests in Europe. Ours are "feral" pigs the mixed breed descendants of mostly domestic stock in the same way our "wild" goats, horses, sheep, cows are.  Any European or Polynesian blood has been diluted to the extreme be 200 years of domestic pig escape and prolific releasing by pig hunters....
Yes it's the domesticated pig gone feral, not the wild boar which wasn't introduced to NZ
